title: 529 plans for education funding
summary: State-sponsored, tax-advantaged accounts for education. Many states offer deductions for contributions to in-state plans.
detailsHtml:
How they work

Contributions grow tax-free; withdrawals are tax-free if used for qualified education expenses (tuition, room/board for at-least-half-time enrollment, books, K-12 tuition up to $10K/year, student loan repayment up to $10K lifetime). Non-qualified withdrawals face income tax plus a 10% penalty on earnings.

State deduction strategy

About 30 states offer state income tax deductions for 529 contributions, typically only for contributions to the state's own plan. Some states have reciprocity ("parity") and allow deductions for any state's plan. If your state offers a deduction, the in-state plan is almost always best despite potentially inferior fund options; the deduction outweighs the fee difference. If your state doesn't, shop nationally — Utah's my529, New York's plan, and California's ScholarShare are widely regarded as best-in-class.

SECURE 2.0 update: Beginning 2024, up to $35,000 of excess 529 funds can be rolled into a Roth IRA in the beneficiary's name, subject to annual IRA contribution limits and a 15-year account-aging requirement. Important second rule (often overlooked): Contributions made within the prior 5 years (and earnings on those contributions) are NOT eligible for rollover, per IRS Notice 2024-2. So a 529 opened in 2010 but with most contributions made in 2024–2025 has limited eligible rollover even if the 15-year clock is satisfied. The beneficiary must also have earned income equal to the rollover amount in the rollover year.
